new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is regularly penultimate; stress can shift to the final syllable in emphatic/emotive utterances (e.g. Allillám), which the orthography marks with an acute accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Emphatic/emotional final stress marked with a written accent (Allillám). Valqui 2020:187, summarizing Quesada 1973, adds emphatic oxytone forms such as [arí] 'sí' and phrases the rule as penultimate 'en palabras de 3 o más sílabas'.
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for the word ('la penúltima sílaba' of the word) in a learner's grammar of the Chetilla/Porcón variety (authors resident 14 years in Chetilla, Cajamarca province); the emphatic shift is described as a discourse/affect effect, not lexical.
new_statements.identity_note: Coombs et al. describe the Quechua of Cajamarca province (Chetilla, Porcón and the Cajamarca valley) = Glottolog caja1238 / ISO qvc; Quesada 1976 covers 'Cajamarca-Cañaris', i.e. also the Ferreñafe/Incahuasi-Cañaris variety (inca1244, ISO quf), which Valqui 2020 lists separately with initial nominal stress, so any statement taken from Quesada 1976 must be checked for which variety it refers to.

new_statements.quote: In most Quechua dialects stress is assigned to the penultimate vowel of each polysyllabic word form and thus provides an easy phonology-based criterion for word delimitation. Exceptionally, in interjections and emphatic expressions, stress can be word-final, e.g. in alalaw 'how cold!'. [...] Vowel loss occurs occasionally, e.g. in Cajamarca wanchi- 'to kill' from *wanu-chi- 'to kill', 'to cause to die'. Several sorts of phonetic reduction, including vowel loss, drastically transformed the phonological appearance of QIIB Chachapoyas Quechua (Taylor 1975, 1994). It appears to be connected with a shift from penultimate to initial word stress, which has occurred in some of the other northern Peruvian dialects as well.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level statement: in most Quechua dialects stress falls on the penultimate vowel of every polysyllabic word (a word-delimitation cue); word-final stress only in interjections and emphatic expressions, in quantity-insensitive dialects on a word-final first-person long vowel, and in Tarma/northern Junin after elision of a final syllable; Pacaraos has phonemic final vs penultimate stress; quantity-insensitive Ancash and quantity-insensitive Cajatambo have initial/weight-dependent patterns. Cajamarca is never given its own stress statement; it appears only as an example of sporadic vowel loss (wanchi-). The shift from penultimate to initial stress is attributed to QIIB Chachapoyas 'and some of the other northern Peruvian dialects', which are not named.
new_statements.exceptions: Word-final stress in interjections and emphatic expressions (alalaw 'how cold!'); quantity-insensitive first-person long vowel keeps final stress; final-syllable elision in Tarma and northern Junin; Pacaraos phonemic final/penultimate contrast; quantity-insensitive Ancash and quantity-insensitive Cajatambo word-initial and syllable-structure-dependent stress; penultimate-to-initial shift in QIIB Chachapoyas and unnamed other northern Peruvian dialects.
new_statements.identity_note: Rimashun kichwapi describes the Quechua of Cajamarca province as spoken in Chetilla and Porcón (front matter names both villages and the authors' consultants from each). Adelaar & Muysken 2004 make a family-level statement ('In most Quechua dialects'); Cajamarca is named in that section only as an example of sporadic vowel loss (wanchi- 'to kill'), and the initial-stress remark concerns QIIB Chachapoyas Quechua.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and same exception type as the catalog record (Coombs, Coombs & Ortiz 2003: penultimate, displaced accent marks emphasis/emotion). It is a pan-Quechua statement rather than a Cajamarca-specific one, but the book's explicit list of deviant-stress northern dialects (Ferreñafe, Amazonas) excludes Cajamarca. This full-text read confirms the compilers snippet reconstruction verbatim (their 'passage B', page then unrecovered, is printed p.198) and fixes the scanned loss (wanči-, not wanchi-/wanci-).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level rule: stress on the penultimate vowel of every polysyllabic word; word-final stress only in interjections/emphatic expressions (alaláw). The book names the northern Peruvian dialects with deviant (non-penultimate) stress as QIIA Ferreñafe and QIIB Amazonas (plus quantity-insensitive Ancash/Cajatambo, Pacaraos, the 16th-c. coastal dialect); Cajamarca (QIIA) is NOT listed among them, so it falls under the general penultimate rule. The p.198 remark that a penult-to-initial shift 'has occurred in some of the other northern Peruvian dialects' (besides Chachapoyas) does not name Cajamarca; read with p.207 it points to Ferreñafe.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing said about secondary stress for Quechua II / Cajamarca
new_statements.exceptions: word-final stress in interjections and emphatic expressions (alaláw 'how cold!'); quantity-insensitive-only: final stress with the first-person long-vowel morpheme and after final-syllable elision (Tarma, N Junín, Pacaraos) - not applicable to Cajamarca
new_statements.identity_note: Adelaar & Muysken treat 'Cajamarca Quechua' as the QIIA dialect of the provinces of Cajamarca and Bambamarca (p.186; Chetilla district named p.404), citing Quesada Castillo 1976a,b; the stress statement itself is pan-Quechua ('most Quechua dialects'), with Cajamarca covered by default rather than by a dialect-specific sentence. The catalog's source (Rimashun kichwapi) describes the Chetilla/Porcón variety.
